svg.title: Pituitary apoplexy and adrenal insufficiency: the symptoms of two emergencies on two separate timelines
svg.desc: Schematic of the two emergencies that can face someone with a pituitary adenoma, drawn as two separate timelines with a third, unrelated postoperative timeline set apart at the bottom. It opens with a statement: this figure carries no doses and no method for adjusting steroids yourself, because how steroids are handled under stress is a clinical question with a standard answer that, including how much and for how long, has to be written down on paper for the patient personally by their endocrinologist. The first axis is pituitary apoplexy. It starts from a sudden severe headache, noted as the commonest and earliest manifestation, with the trigger from the 2016 Society for Endocrinology endocrine emergency guidance: consider pituitary apoplexy in anyone with an acute severe headache plus any one of the following - those in whom subarachnoid haemorrhage and meningitis have been excluded, those with neuro-ophthalmic signs, and those with a known pituitary tumour. Four branches come off that start point: ophthalmoplegia from involvement of the cavernous sinus, most commonly a third nerve palsy with a drooping eyelid, double vision and pupil changes; reduced visual acuity and visual field defects from compression of the optic chiasm, most commonly a bitemporal hemianopia in which the outer field of each eye seems covered over; fever, neck stiffness, photophobia or reduced consciousness, which can look very like subarachnoid haemorrhage or meningitis; and nausea and vomiting alongside the headache. The four branches converge on a single action: go to the emergency department the same day, without waiting for a clinic appointment and without driving yourself, having a relative take you or calling an ambulance, and at triage saying the words "I have a pituitary tumour" or "possible pituitary apoplexy", because the guidance lists a known pituitary tumour as one of the triggers. Beside the axis is the list of precipitants - hypertension, major surgery, dynamic testing of the pituitary gland, anticoagulation, coagulopathy, pregnancy and head trauma - and three facts: about four in five of these people had no idea anything was wrong with their pituitary beforehand and the symptoms resemble commoner neurological conditions; MRI is the imaging of choice and the guidance states it confirmed the diagnosis in more than nine in ten patients, with CT used only when MRI cannot be done; and in the Banbury community study 5 of 63 patients with a pituitary adenoma (7.9%) were found through a typical pituitary apoplexy, which is the proportion diagnosed by presenting with apoplexy and not the proportion of people with a pituitary tumour who will later have one, the denominators being different. The axis ends with the order of management in the emergency department: stabilise first; empirical steroid replacement for those who are haemodynamically unstable, whose consciousness is altered or whose visual acuity or fields are severely affected, which the guidance calls potentially lifesaving; and urgent referral to a joint neurosurgical and endocrine team. The second axis is adrenal insufficiency, far slower and far easier to miss - tired, no strength, dizzy on standing, until a febrile illness one day brings the whole thing down. Its symptoms are grouped in five cells: whole body - fatigue, lack of energy, weight loss; blood pressure - low blood pressure, postural dizziness and hypotension, collapse, hypovolaemic shock in severe cases; abdomen - abdominal pain, tenderness on pressing, nausea and vomiting; fever and consciousness - fever, confusion, somnolence, delirium or coma in severe cases; and back and legs - cramps or spasms, with the guidance noting specifically that this one is easily chased as some other problem. A further cell covers the skin: pituitary in origin, that is secondary, is ticked and the skin is pale, described in the guidance as an alabaster-like complexion; darkening of the skin is crossed out as belonging to primary adrenal insufficiency and not to the pituitary kind. The same cell records that in more than half of people with adrenal insufficiency the diagnosis is only made after an acute crisis, so for anyone with a pituitary tumour "is this axis doing enough" is a question to ask actively rather than to wait for symptoms to answer. A red line adds that anyone already on steroid replacement who is vomiting or has diarrhoea to the point where tablets will not stay down, or who becomes confused or cannot stand, is in an emergency and should go to the emergency department the same day with their medication list, rather than sitting it out at home. Stress situations are drawn as four questions to have answered before becoming ill: when I am ill or febrile enough to need bed rest or antibiotics, what should happen to my steroid, please write it down for me; and when I am vomiting or have diarrhoea and cannot keep the tablets down, what then and who do I call; before an operation, a general anaesthetic or bowel preparation for a colonoscopy, who should I tell and how far ahead; and do I need an injection kept at home, who will teach me and my family to use it and how often should we check it has not expired. The panel explains that these four match what the guidance lists as the clinician's responsibilities - educating patient and family, teaching self-injection and supplying the emergency injection, regular review and a set of emergency phone numbers - and adds two pieces of hardware, a steroid emergency card and a medical alert bracelet, the card to be carried at all times and shown to any healthcare professional, its official function being to prompt the staff taking over and its use being for adults aged sixteen and over, with no citable statement found on whether Taiwan has an equivalent scheme. At the foot of the figure a clear divider sets apart a third thing, labelled "what follows is a different thing": the timeline after surgery, not to be remembered alongside the two emergencies above. Diabetes insipidus - in a series of 881 transsphenoidal operations, among the 857 without it beforehand, 18.3% had it immediately after surgery, while permanent diabetes insipidus needing long-term treatment was only 2%. Hyponatraemia - something that happens after discharge, with 31.9% overall and 6.4% readmission in the free-fluid group of a randomised trial of 300 patients. The figure closes with a piece of paper folded into a wallet: the diagnosis, the hormone replacement being taken, the endocrinologist and their phone number, and the answers to those four questions, folded into the wallet and photographed for the family, to be handed over at the next clinic visit for a few words to be added - what it is there to stop being not the tumour but the sequence in which the diagnosis only arrives after the collapse.

g.text: TWO EMERGENCIES, TWO SEPARATE TIMELINES
One happens within hours; the other is quiet enough to be
mistaken for tiredness
This figure is about the two emergencies that can face someone with a pituitary adenoma. The two axes are different things and must not
be remembered as one: pituitary apoplexy above, adrenal insufficiency below.
The strip at the very bottom is the fluid problem after surgery, which is not on the same timeline as either emergency.
This figure carries no doses and no method for adjusting steroids yourself - how steroids are handled under stress is a clinical question with a standard
answer, and that answer, including how much and for how long, has to be written down on paper for you personally by your endocrinologist.
First axis: pituitary apoplexy
The 2016 endocrine emergency guidance of the Society for Endocrinology writes the trigger very concretely: consider pituitary apoplexy in anyone with an acute
severe headache plus any one of the following - those in whom subarachnoid haemorrhage and meningitis have been excluded, those with neuro-ophthalmic signs, and
those with a known pituitary tumour.
A sudden severe headache
Acute severe headache is the commonest and earliest manifestation
plus any one of these
Ophthalmoplegia
involvement of the cavernous sinus
Most commonly a third nerve
palsy
Drooping eyelid, double vision,
pupil changes
Reduced visual acuity and visual
field defects
compression of the optic chiasm
Most commonly a bitemporal
hemianopia
The outer field of each eye seems
covered over
Fever, neck stiffness,
photophobia or reduced
consciousness
looks like something else
Can look very like subarachnoid
haemorrhage or meningitis
Nausea and vomiting
often alongside the headache
The headache may be
accompanied by nausea and
vomiting
Once you recognise this combination there is only one action: go to the emergency department the same day
Do not wait for a clinic appointment and do not drive yourself; have a relative take you or call an ambulance. At triage, say the words "I have a pituitary tumour"
or "possible pituitary apoplexy" - the guidance lists a known pituitary tumour as one of the triggers, and saying so changes the order things happen in.
The list of precipitants
Hypertension
Major surgery
Dynamic testing of the pituitary gland
Anticoagulation
Coagulopathy
Pregnancy
Head trauma
Four in five
About four in five of these people had no idea there
was anything wrong with their pituitary
beforehand, and the symptoms look like commoner
neurological conditions
More than nine in ten
MRI is the imaging of choice, and the guidance
states that it confirmed the diagnosis in more than
nine in ten patients; CT is used only when MRI
cannot be done
5 of 63
In the community study in Banbury, 5 of 63 patients
with a pituitary adenoma (7.9%) were found through
a typical pituitary apoplexy - that is the proportion
diagnosed by presenting with apoplexy, not the
proportion of people with a pituitary tumour who
will later have one; the denominators are different
What happens in the emergency department, in the order the same document sets out
Stabilise first
Empirical steroid replacement for those who are haemodynamically unstable, whose consciousness is altered, or whose visual acuity or fields are severely
affected - the guidance calls it potentially lifesaving
Urgent referral to a joint neurosurgical and endocrine team
Second axis: adrenal insufficiency
Far slower, and far easier to miss. Tired, no strength, dizzy on standing - until a febrile illness one day brings the whole thing down.
Whole body
Fatigue
Lack of energy
Weight loss
Blood pressure
Low blood pressure
Postural dizziness and hypotension
Collapse
Hypovolaemic shock in severe cases
Abdomen
Abdominal pain
Tenderness on pressing
Nausea and vomiting
Fever and consciousness
Fever
Confusion
Somnolence
Delirium or coma in severe cases
Back and legs
Cramps or spasms
The guidance notes specifically that this one is
easily chased as some other problem
One feature that patient leaflets often get the wrong way round
Pituitary in origin (secondary)
The skin is pale - the guidance describes an alabaster-like complexion
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Darkening of the skin belongs to primary adrenal insufficiency, not to the
pituitary kind
In more than half of people with adrenal insufficiency, the diagnosis is only made after an acute crisis. So if you have a pituitary tumour, "is this axis of mine
doing enough" is a question to ask actively, not one to wait for symptoms to answer.
If you are already on steroid replacement and you are vomiting or having diarrhoea to the point where the tablets will not stay down, or you become
confused or cannot stand, that is an emergency: go to the emergency department the same day and take your medication list with you. Do not sit it out at
home because "it is probably just a stomach bug".
Under stress: four questions to have answered before you are ill
These four are not my invention; they match what the guidance lists as the clinician's responsibilities - educating the patient and family, teaching self-injection and
supplying the emergency injection, regular review, and a set of emergency phone numbers.
When I am ill or febrile enough to need bed rest or antibiotics, what
should happen to my steroid? Please write it down for me.
And when I am vomiting or having diarrhoea and simply cannot keep
the tablets down - what then, and who do I call?
Before an operation, a general anaesthetic or bowel preparation for
a colonoscopy, who should I tell and how far ahead?
Do I need an injection kept at home? Who will teach me and my family
to use it, and how often should we check it has not expired?
Two pieces of hardware as well: the Society for Endocrinology recommends giving patients a steroid emergency card and encourages wearing a medical alert bracelet,
with the card carried at all times and shown to any healthcare professional; the official page explains that its function is to prompt the staff taking over, and that it is for
adults aged sixteen and over. Whether Taiwan has an equivalent official card scheme, I could find no citable statement - ask your endocrinologist or your case manager.
What follows is a different thing
The timeline after surgery is not to be remembered alongside the two emergencies above
Diabetes insipidus
In a series of 881 transsphenoidal operations, among the 857 without diabetes
insipidus beforehand, 18.3% had it immediately after surgery
Permanent diabetes insipidus needing long-term treatment was only 2%
Hyponatraemia
Hyponatraemia is something that happens after discharge
In a randomised trial of 300 patients, the free-fluid group had hyponatraemia
overall in 31.9% and readmission in 6.4%
A piece of paper folded into your wallet
Write down the diagnosis, the hormone replacement you are on, your endocrinologist and their phone number, and the answers to those four questions; fold it into
your wallet and photograph it for your family. At the next clinic visit, hand it over for a few words to be added. What it is there to stop is not the tumour - it is the
sequence where the diagnosis only arrives after the collapse.
Schematic, redrawn from the two 2016 Society for Endocrinology emergency guidance documents on pituitary apoplexy and adrenal crisis (Baldeweg 2016, Arlt 2016),
Fernandez 2010, Nemergut 2005 and the 2025 randomised trial of postoperative fluid restriction, rather than reproduced from their figures; the cohorts, designs and
endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data points must not be compared directly. The figure contains no dose and no method of dose adjustment.
